title: The Attic Decontamination Process, Step by Step
h1: What Is the Attic Decontamination Process?
description: Attic decontamination removes rodent waste, soiled insulation and debris, sanitizes the space and seals entry points. Here is each step and what to expect.
quick_answer: Attic decontamination is the process of removing contaminated insulation, rodent droppings, nesting material and debris from an attic, then sanitizing the surfaces, sealing pest entry points and installing fresh insulation. It is usually needed after a rodent infestation, but it can also follow water damage, smoke exposure or years of buildup.
body:
The attic is easy to forget about until something goes wrong. Rats and mice move in, a roof leak soaks the insulation, or smoke from a wildfire works its way in. When that happens, the insulation can't simply be topped off. Contaminated material needs to come out, the space needs to be cleaned, and the reason it happened needs to be fixed.

When do you need attic decontamination?

  • Rodent activity. Droppings, urine, nesting material and chewed insulation, along with scratching sounds overhead at night.
  • Odors. A musty, ammonia-like or stale smell coming from the ceiling, closets or HVAC registers.
  • Water damage. Insulation that's been soaked by a roof or plumbing leak, which can mat down and grow mold.
  • Smoke or soot. Smoke from a wildfire or a house fire can leave residue and odors in insulation.
  • Old, compressed insulation. Years of foot traffic, storage or settling that have left insulation thin and dirty.

In many Southern California homes, the furnace and much of the ductwork sit in the attic. That means whatever is in the attic can affect the air your HVAC system moves through the house, especially if the ducts are leaky.

What happens during attic decontamination?

  1. Inspection. We look at the insulation, the extent of contamination, signs of active pests, entry points, ducts and the condition of the roof deck and framing.
  2. Protecting the home. The work area and path through the house are covered, and the attic access is sealed off to keep dust out of living spaces.
  3. Insulation removal. Contaminated insulation, droppings and nesting material are removed with a commercial vacuum system that carries debris directly to a collection bag outside the home.
  4. Cleaning. Remaining debris is cleared from the joists, top plates and other surfaces.
  5. Sanitizing. An appropriate disinfectant or deodorizer is applied to treat affected surfaces and reduce odors.
  6. Sealing entry points. Gaps at vents, rooflines, pipes and other openings are sealed or screened to keep rodents from getting back in.
  7. Air sealing. Gaps around light fixtures, top plates and penetrations into the living space can be sealed before new insulation goes in.
  8. New insulation. Fresh insulation is installed to the depth recommended for the home.

Why does sealing entry points matter so much?

Cleaning an attic without closing up the way rodents got in means you'll likely be cleaning it again. Rats and mice can squeeze through surprisingly small openings, often around roof vents, gaps where the roof meets the walls, utility penetrations and torn vent screens. Sealing those openings is what makes the cleanup last. If there's an active infestation, pest control should handle trapping before or during the work.

Is it safe to clean an attic yourself?

We don't recommend it. Rodent droppings and urine can carry diseases, and disturbing them sends dust into the air. Attics are also hot, cramped, full of nails and wiring, and easy to step through between the joists. Professional crews use protective gear, containment and specialized vacuum equipment to keep contaminants out of the living space.

What happens if you leave a contaminated attic alone?

Soiled insulation doesn't fix itself. Rodent urine and droppings keep producing odors, and an active infestation keeps adding more. Rodents also chew wiring, flex ducts and insulation, which can lead to electrical hazards and air leaks that drive up energy use. Matted or wet insulation loses much of its ability to slow heat flow, so upstairs rooms get hotter in summer and colder on winter nights. The longer the problem goes, the bigger the cleanup tends to be.

What should you check after the work?

After decontamination, keep an ear out for scratching or movement in the ceiling, and look for new droppings in the garage or around the attic access. Odors should fade within a short time. If your ducts run through the attic, it's worth having them inspected too, since damaged or leaky ducts can pull contaminants into the system.

Our attic cleaning and insulation service covers inspection, removal, sanitizing, rodent proofing, air sealing and new insulation. If ducts were affected, our duct cleaning and repair team can help.
faqs: How long does attic decontamination take?
Many attics take a day or two, depending on size, how much insulation needs to come out and whether new insulation goes in during the same visit. Your estimate will include a timeline.
Can I stay home during attic cleaning?
In most cases, yes. The crew contains the work area and routes debris outside through vacuum hoses. Some homeowners with breathing sensitivities prefer to be out during removal.
Do I need to replace all of my attic insulation after rodents?
Not always. If contamination is limited to a small area, spot removal may be enough. Widespread droppings, urine or nesting usually mean full removal is the better choice.
Will attic decontamination get rid of the smell?
Removing soiled insulation and debris and sanitizing the surfaces takes care of the source of most odors. A lingering smell can mean contamination elsewhere, such as in walls or ducts.
